caption: Relationship profiling means reaching across more than one database object at once.

eyebrow: Which database a query runs against
caption: The toolbar database selector — relevant whenever a relationship check needs a specific, non-default database.
Recent connections often point straight at the sample databases, like AdventureWorks, this course's examples use.

code:
SELECT
    soh.SalesOrderID,
    soh.CustomerID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
LEFT JOIN Sales.Customer c
    ON soh.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE c.CustomerID IS NULL;
caption: Every row returned points at a CustomerID that doesn't exist in Customer — an orphaned row.

code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphaned_orders
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
LEFT JOIN Sales.Customer c
    ON soh.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE c.CustomerID IS NULL;
caption: The exact number you'd report as a referential integrity finding — Lesson 19 turns this into a formal rule.

code:
SELECT
    EmailAddress,
    CASE
        WHEN EmailAddress LIKE '%_@_%._%' THEN 'Looks valid'
        ELSE 'Does not match expected pattern'
    END AS pattern_check
FROM Sales.Customer
WHERE EmailAddress IS NOT NULL;
caption: A fast read on shape, not a full email spec — is this worth a stricter rule later?

code:
SELECT pattern_check, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM (
    SELECT CASE
        WHEN EmailAddress LIKE '%_@_%._%' THEN 'Looks valid'
        ELSE 'Does not match expected pattern'
    END AS pattern_check
    FROM Sales.Customer
    WHERE EmailAddress IS NOT NULL
) t
GROUP BY pattern_check;
caption: 9,812 valid vs. 188 not — the scale of the problem, in one query.
